passage:
When Ira got off the bus from school, Minakshi came out of the shop to greet her, arms open. Ira, fourteen, stepped sideways and ducked into the house. "Hi, Ma."
Minakshi let her arms drop. Inside, Ira kicked off her shoes and felt a strange tug. She didn't want the hug. But she didn't want Ma to stop wanting to give it either.
That evening Ira sat on the back step, scrolling. Minakshi came out with two glasses of lassi and sat down beside her, not too close. She didn't say anything about the hug. She just handed over a glass.
They watched the buffaloes come home down the lane. After a while, Ira leaned her head on Minakshi's shoulder, just for a moment.
"Good day?" Minakshi asked.
"Okay day," Ira said.

qa.q: What did Minakshi bring out to the back step?
qa.a: She brought out two glasses of lassi.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling after stepping away from the hug?
qa.a: Ira felt a strange tug of mixed feelings: she didn't want the hug, but didn't want her mother to stop offering it.

qa.q: What did Minakshi do that kept the connection alive?
qa.a: She respected Ira's space, sat beside her without mentioning the hug, and let Ira come closer in her own time.

qa.q: How might Minakshi have felt when Ira stepped sideways?
qa.a: She probably felt a little hurt and surprised, which is why she let her arms drop.

grounding: It shows a teenager who avoids a mother's hug while still craving warmth, and a mother who respects her pace by sitting beside her instead.

passage:
Parent's note to myself, after a hard week
For the last few months, my fifteen-year-old, Pema, has gone stiff every time I hug her. Arms straight down, face turned away. It hurt me more than I've admitted. On Tuesday I hugged her in front of her friends and she pulled away sharply. That night I realised I was hugging for me, not for her. So I've changed. I ask, 'Hug or no hug?' and I accept 'no' without a sigh. I sit beside her on the sofa during her show and pat her knee when I leave. Tonight she leaned her head on my shoulder for five minutes, without saying anything. I didn't move. I'm keeping the door open. She'll come when she's ready.
Chandrika

qa.q: How long did Pema lean her head on Chandrika's shoulder?
qa.a: Five minutes.

qa.q: How did Chandrika feel when Pema stiffened at hugs?
qa.a: Chandrika felt hurt, more than had been admitted.

qa.q: What did Chandrika change that kept connection alive?
qa.a: Asking before hugging, accepting no, sitting beside Pema and patting her knee.

qa.q: How might Pema feel when her mother asks 'Hug or no hug?'
qa.a: Pema probably feels respected and less pressured, which makes it easier to come closer.

grounding: Shows a teenager stiffening at family hugs while still wanting warmth, and a parent respecting her pace and offering gentler closeness.

passage:
Sunday
Mum hugged me at the school gate today, right in front of Rohit and Kabir. I pulled away and said, 'Mum, not here!' She looked really hurt. I felt bad all afternoon. It's not that I don't like her. I just feel weird being hugged now, like I'm six. But I also kind of miss it? When I had flu last month, she sat on the edge of my bed and rubbed my back and it was the best thing.
Tonight she knocked and said, 'I'm sorry about the gate. What works for you? Pat on the head? Just sitting here?' I said just sitting. So she sat on my bed while I did my maths, and before she left she squeezed my shoulder. That was nice.
Eshaan

qa.q: Where did Mum hug Eshaan?
qa.a: At the school gate.

qa.q: How did Eshaan feel after pulling away?
qa.a: Eshaan felt bad and guilty, since Mum looked really hurt.

qa.q: What did Mum do that respected Eshaan's pace?
qa.a: She apologised and asked what worked, then sat nearby and squeezed a shoulder instead of hugging.

qa.q: How might Mum have felt at the school gate?
qa.a: She probably felt hurt and embarrassed, but then chose to ask rather than insist.

grounding: Shows a teenager pulling away from a parent's hug while still craving warmth, and a parent respecting that pace and offering other closeness.

passage: When the bus from the district school dropped Gargi at the Ranipur crossing, Rehana was waiting as always, arms open. Gargi stepped round the hug and fixed her bag strap. "Not here, Ammi. Everyone's looking." Rehana's arms fell. At home Gargi went straight to the roof. Rehana stood at the stove a long time, stirring nothing. That evening she didn't push. She carried two cups of tea up to the roof and sat beside Gargi on the parapet, shoulders not quite touching, watching the goats come home. After a while Gargi leaned her head on her mother's shoulder, just for a moment. Rehana kept very still and said only, "The tea's getting cold."

qa.q: Where did Rehana carry the two cups of tea?
qa.a: Up to the roof.

qa.q: Why did Gargi step round the hug at the bus stop?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and self-conscious with everyone looking, and wanted her own space.

qa.q: What did Rehana do that kept the connection alive?
qa.a: She didn't push, sat beside Gargi with tea, and let Gargi come closer at her own pace.

qa.q: How did Rehana feel when her arms fell?
qa.a: She felt hurt and a bit lost, standing at the stove stirring nothing.

grounding: Shows a teenager stiffening at a public hug while still wanting warmth, and a parent respecting her pace by sitting beside her and keeping closeness on offer.
